stem: You're about to dial Maria, who owns a two-store retail business. Companies House shows she opened the second store in January. Which opener works as an M1 diagnostic?

choices.text: Hi Maria — do you have a moment to talk about your corporate spending?
choices.feedback: It mentions no signal and asks nothing Maria could answer. When P.B. used it on GC-19, she hung up at 0:08.

choices.text: Our card is cheaper than your bank's — worth 10 minutes?
choices.feedback: Talking about fees turns the opening into a pitch, and the only answer it leaves Maria is no.

choices.text: We help SMB owners get real-time visibility into their team spend — can I tell you more?
choices.feedback: This goes straight into a pitch before anyone has asked Maria anything, and it leaves her nothing to answer.

choices.text: I noticed you opened a second store in January — who's approving card spend across both stores now?
choices.feedback: It names the second store and asks who controls the spending. M.G. opened GC-01 this way and booked the demo on the same call.

stem: Tom has closed a Series B, announced in April, and his company of 22 people has posted six engineering jobs. Which opening question pairs that signal with a question about who controls what, in 15 words or fewer?

choices.text: Saw your Series B — who's owning per-employee card issuance now that engineering is scaling?
choices.feedback: In 14 words it names the Series B and asks who owns per-employee card issuance. L.D. opened his call with Tom on GC-06 in much the same way.

choices.text: Congratulations on the Series B — that must be a huge milestone for the team. Would love to hear how it's going.
choices.feedback: It is too long, and it only compliments Tom without asking who controls the spending.

choices.text: We help fast-growing SaaS teams with corporate cards — sound like something you'd want to evaluate?
choices.feedback: This is a pitch without a signal, like the 'We help SMB owners' opener in question 1.
It is a yes-or-no question with no signal behind it. Even if Tom says yes, you have nothing to build on.

stem: You have asked your diagnostic question, and the buyer has said nothing for six seconds, without a breath or a word on the line. What do you do?

choices.text: Rephrase the question more clearly so they understand it.
choices.feedback: Rephrasing takes the silence away at the moment the buyer is working out an answer.

choices.text: Wait. Let the buyer fill the silence.
choices.feedback: The buyer is thinking during those seconds. What they say when they break the silence is usually the real problem.

choices.text: Fill the gap with a quick benefit statement to keep momentum.
choices.feedback: P.B. does this on his calls. Pitching into the silence throws away the answer your question was meant to get.

choices.text: Ask if they're still on the line.
choices.feedback: Asking whether they are still there breaks the silence and tells the buyer you are uncomfortable with it.
